name: Shibuya
description: Shibuya, Harajuku and Yoyogi Park, out to Sangenjaya's backstreets: the scramble and Hachiko, the city from SHIBUYA SKY, Center Gai's arcades and the streets a famous game drew.

imagery.attribution: Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (GSI) seamless aerial photographs (GSI terms of use, source attribution)

plateau.veg_note: PLATEAU's Shibuya-ku survey of single trees has one mesh (53393596), south of the map; the street trees take the heights of Tokyo's surveyed ones (pipeline/plateau_veg.py)
plateau.attribution: MLIT Project PLATEAU Tokyo 23 wards LOD2 building models (CC BY 4.0), as vector tiles by indigo-lab (MIT)

water.note: No sea. The Shibuya River runs in a culvert under the station; its open stretch south of it and the Meguro River from Ikejiri-Ohashi down through Nakameguro are concrete channels drawn at their own level (inland, pipeline/inland_water.py), and so are the parks' ponds.

inland.note: Concrete revetments about 4.5-5 m from the street down to a shallow flow (read from photographs, not measured); the Meguro about 9 m between its walls at Ikejiri-Ohashi and 13 m at Nakameguro, the Shibuya River about 8 m. The ponds at the 5 m laser survey's level.

roofs.note: pipeline/arcades.py (#234): two low PLATEAU-only solids in pedestrian squares (tools/square_huts.py) that the aerial photograph shows are canopies, not huts: a covered walk 3 m wide and 4.1 m tall along the footway by the Yamanote tracks north of the station, and a 2.6 m shelter on an island of the east exit's bus terminal. Each is named by a point inside it, as PLATEAU's footprints have no OSM id.

susuki.note: Susuki (trees.json susuki, #326): on the open grassland and meadows OpenStreetMap maps (natural=grassland, landuse=meadow: the unmown grass of the parks and the hills, where susuki is the grass that stands) (Overture base land, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; pipeline/grasses.py). Its heads stand from mid August to spring (web/trees.js).

trees.note: Species are not mapped; the mix is a guess from the cities' street-tree surveys and the parks' own guides: ginkgo and zelkova (keyaki) are Japan's commonest street trees, with plane trees and camphor; the woods are the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves and camphors, with zelkovas, black pines, maples and a few cedars (sugi, standing for hinoki too). Areas give the parks and precincts known for their own trees a mix of their own; their outlines are OpenStreetMap's (pipeline/tree_areas.py). Somei-yoshino cherries (sakura) line Tokyo's streets after the ginkgo and the zelkova, and stand in the parks' lawns and along the rivers and moats; areas give the places known for them a mix of their own.

areas.name: Hachiko Square's planters
areas.note: The round planter north of Hachiko holds a Somei-yoshino (photographs 2020-25).

areas.name: Hachiko Square's planters, south
areas.note: And so does the one south of him.

areas.name: Meguro River
areas.note: About 800 cherries on both banks from Ikejiri-Ohashi down through Nakameguro, their branches over the water (Meguro City). In the bloom pink chochin hang along both railings and the cherries are lit after dark (#241): the area is the river's line buffered 14 m, so the railings, about 5.5 m either side of it, are 8.5 m inside the outline.

areas.name: Meiji Jingu
areas.note: The planted shrine forest, now mostly camphor and the evergreen oaks and shii of the laurel forest.

tour.title: Sangenjaya to Harajuku
tour.text: Youth culture's Tokyo: fashion on Takeshita Street, the forest of Meiji Jingu, the busiest crossing on Earth, and out west the izakaya alleys of Sangenjaya where the city goes home to drink.

tour.title: The scramble
tour.text: When the lights change, every crossing turns green at once, the diagonals too, and up to three thousand people cross together. Watch it from above, then join in. Hachiko sits to the south, waiting for his master, as he did for ten years.

tour.title: SHIBUYA SKY, 229 m
tour.text: An open-air deck on Scramble Square's roof, glass at the edge and nothing above you but sky. Come at sunset: Mount Fuji on the horizon, then Tokyo lighting up beneath your feet.

tour.title: Sangenjaya's triangle
tour.text: Between Setagaya-dori and Route 246: a bathhouse, a snack bar, a meat shop open all night. A game drew its hero's home town here and called it Yongen-Jaya; fans still come looking for the café.

protection.title: No sun-access rule for public places
protection.summary: Tokyo protects no park's sunlight. The windows are a lunch-hour thought experiment for this project, as in the Marunouchi model.
protection.source_note: Windows are our own choice (noon to 13:00, all year), not law. The Building Standards Act's shadow rule (日影規制, art. 56-2) limits hours of shadow on neighbouring land in residential-type zones; it does not cover public places and does not apply in commercial districts such as Shibuya.
protection.reading_note: Tokyo keeps standard time all year. Miyashita Park is a roof garden on a mall (2020): its sun here is read at the ground, so treat it with care.
protection.tip: Tip: try a tower on the block south of Yoyogi Park, west of Harajuku Station.

crowd.note: hours: the share of the peak crowd out, by the hour: the morning commute, lunch, and the evening, busiest from 18:00 to 21:00 and busier still on Friday and Saturday nights and at the weekend (Shibuya Redevelopment Association, 2014: 260,000 people a day on weekdays, 390,000 on holidays); few after the last trains (about 00:30)

lines.title: Report back
lines.on_open: Every walk done. Report back to Aoi by QFRONT, across the scramble from Hachiko.

quests.title: Hachiko
talk: ようこそ渋谷へ! I'm Aoi. I guide pilgrims: people who come to stand where a story stood. This month it's ten years since a film and a game put these streets on the map.

You've just crossed it: the scramble, up to three thousand people at one change of the lights. Hachiko, back across the road, has sat there since 1948, and a game called his square Station Square. Cross back to him when the lights change.
Want to see it from above? The lift at SKY GATE in Scramble Square, just across the road, goes up to SHIBUYA SKY, and a helicopter waits on the roof. A hand up at the kerb (Y) stops a taxi.

steps.text: Meet Shun at the mouth of Center Gai

quests.title: Center Gai
talk: Center Gai. A game called it Central Street and gave it a burger bar that doesn't exist. The arch is real: go and read it.
See the glass passage over the crossing, on the station side? Okamoto Taro's thirty-metre mural, Myth of Tomorrow, hangs inside. A game made that passage a hideout.
For the view everyone came for, go up SHIBUYA SKY on top of Scramble Square. Yuna works the door.

steps.text: Read the arch over Center Gai
Find Yuna at SHIBUYA SKY's street door

quests.title: SHIBUYA SKY
talk: SKY GATE: the lifts run from 14F to 45F at 360 metres a minute. From the 46th floor an escalator takes you out into the open air.
The roof is about 2,500 square metres. The glass is lowest at SKY EDGE, over the scramble. No bags past 46F: the wind takes them.
Press E by the lift door. Or open the map: the roof is on your list of places to go.

steps.text: Ride the escalator out onto the roof
Stand at SKY EDGE, over the scramble

quests.title: SKY EDGE
talk: From up here the scramble is a clock face: everyone waits, then everyone goes.
GEO COMPASS, the raised deck in the middle, points at places you can't see: Mt Fuji, Skytree, Suga Shrine, even Paris and Sydney.
After dark, CROSSING LIGHT: eighteen searchlights. {sun_line}

quests.title: Sangenjaya
talk: Sangenjaya, three tea houses. In a game it's Yongen-Jaya, four: the same backstreets with one more tea house.
The game's café has the front of a snack bar here, New Marina. The bathhouse is Chiyo-no-yu, across the lane.
Take it slow. These are people's homes and small shops.

quests.title: Chiyo-no-yu
talk: Forty years a regular. The curtain says ゆ: hot water. Men on one side, women on the other.
Coin laundry beside it, vending machines out front. Everything a backstreet needs.
Come back after dark. The signs light up the triangle between Setagaya-dori and Route 246.

quests.title: Pilgrim
talk: お帰り! A crossing, a bathhouse, a roof 229 metres up. All of it real, and now you've stood in all of it.

Ten years ago a game drew these streets. Now you've walked them. The stairs of Your Name are in Shinjuku: two stops north on the Yamanote Line, and my friend Nao guides there. Or change the time, go up SHIBUYA SKY at night, or just wander.

overture.note: The overture (docs/OVERTURE.md, web/game/overture.js): Crossing. A petal (a ginkgo leaf in autumn, a snowflake in winter, a mote of light in summer) leaves the edge of SHIBUYA SKY, falls 229 m to the scramble, passes Hachiko, and the screens, and ends on the scramble from across it, into the sun, before the game begins at the kerb (game.start). Crowds are kept at a distance: no shot comes close to them. Points name the landmarks in scene.json, so a rebuilt map moves them.

caption.text: The wind on the roof of Scramble Square, above the busiest crossing in the world.
He met his master's train here every evening, and went on waiting for nine years after he was gone.

night.note: After dark: a meteor crosses the sky over Shibuya's lights, from the stars down to the skyline, as a film's trailer would show the city. Every shot is from the air or across the city; none comes near the crowd.
